blocks.title: <ico-recycle></ico-recycle> EPISODE RECAP · from B2
blocks.intro: Before we go on air: five formal phrases from the end of B2. Match each one with its everyday version.

blocks.title: <ico-book></ico-book> WORD PARTNERS
blocks.intro: At C1 your grammar is rarely the problem. What gives you away is the word partner: the verb, adverb or adjective a native speaker expects next to a word. Five steps, then ten idioms and the rule for using them.

vocab.sp: to say that something worries you
to decide what the facts mean
to do something that might go wrong
almost certainly not going to happen
a lot of cars, moving slowly

blocks.note: How it works: flashcards , memory, listening , gap-fill , compare and a dialogue. Press CHECK wherever you see it.

parts.html: 1 · WHAT A COLLOCATION IS — not grammar, not logic: habit

items.en: We got stuck in heavy traffic.
items.sp: Not strong traffic, not big traffic. Nothing explains it; English speakers just say it this way.

items.en: He has a strong accent.
There's a slim chance of rain.
items.sp: And a small chance is slim.

parts.html: 2 · MAKE, DO, TAKE, HAVE — four small verbs, four sets of partners

items: make an effort · a mistake · a decision
take a risk · a break · notes
have a look · a word · doubts

items.en: I made an effort to arrive early.
We did some research on tonight's guest.
items.sp: do + research (uncountable: some research, never a research).

items.en: She took a risk and changed careers.
Let's have a look at the script.

parts.html: 3 · THREE MORE VERB PARTNERS — the ones you hear on the news

items.en: Listeners raised concerns about the new schedule.
We always meet our deadlines.
What conclusion did you draw?

parts.html: 4 · INTENSIFIERS THAT PAIR — «very» always works; these sound like C1

items.en: It's highly unlikely.
I was bitterly disappointed.
We're deeply concerned.
That's perfectly normal.

parts.html: 5 · IDIOMS: ONE PER PARAGRAPH — and no clichés on air

items.en: You'll have to hit the ground running.
items.sp: One idiom, in the right place: it sounds natural.

items.en: At the end of the day, we need to think outside the box.
items.sp: Two tired clichés in one sentence. Listeners stop listening.

parts.body: The rule of one. An idiom is seasoning: one per paragraph adds flavor, three is a costume. Idioms are informal, so keep them out of contracts and formal emails.

parts.html: SPANISH TRAP — los compañeros de palabra que el español cambia

items.en: Can I ask a question?
items.sp: «Hacer una pregunta» = ask a question, nunca make.

items.en: I made a mistake.
items.sp: «Cometer un error» = make a mistake, nunca do.

items.en: That makes sense.
She earns good money.
items.sp: «Ganar dinero» trabajando = earn. Win es para premios y partidos.

items.en: I met someone new at the party.
items.sp: «Conocer a alguien» por primera vez = meet, no know.

items.en: We drove home in heavy rain.

parts.body: make a question → ask a question · do a mistake → make a mistake · it has sense → it makes sense · strong rain → heavy rain

blocks.title: <ico-star></ico-star> ON AIR
blocks.intro:
Your first day at The Signal, the city's talk-radio show. You are the new producer's assistant. Roz, the producer, hands you a headset: «You hit the ground running here.» Tonight's guest, Sam, changed careers at forty.

WORDS OF THE DAY (they must appear in your writing): candid = honest, even when it is uncomfortable · hit the ground running · take a risk.

blocks.title: TEN IDIOMS · tap to flip
blocks.intro: Say what you think it means before you flip the card. Five of them are in tonight's interview.

cards.back: start something new at full speed · «She hit the ground running on day one.»
a lot to learn in a short time · «The first month was a steep learning curve.»
do something badly to save time or money · «They cut corners, and it shows.»
the obvious problem nobody mentions · «Let's talk about the elephant in the room.»
starting again from the beginning · «The plan failed, so it's back to square one.»
in agreement about what to do · «Are we all on the same page?»
something that changes a situation completely · «The new studio is a game changer.»
decide as things happen, without a plan · «No script tonight. Let's play it by ear.»
a small visible part of a bigger problem · «These complaints are the tip of the iceberg.»
something bad that turns out to be good · «Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.»

blocks.title: MEMORY · idiom and plain meaning
blocks.intro: Find each idiom and what it means in plain English. Tap two cards.

pairs.b: do it badly to save time
bad luck that turns out well

blocks.title: AUDIO 1 · THE INTERVIEW
blocks.desc: Nora interviews Sam, who left accounting at forty to open a bakery. Listen for the word partners: there are eight collocations and several idioms.

questions.q: What does "a steep learning curve" refer to in Sam's story?
options: Learning to bake in large quantities
Learning to read a balance sheet
Learning to speak on the radio

questions.q: What was the big risk Sam took?
options: Leaving a safe job to open a bakery
Yes: the lost salary still hurts
No: the money is worse, but the work is better

questions.q: Which phrase does Nora use to raise the uncomfortable topic?

speaking.prompt: Retell Sam's story in four sentences. Use two collocations and one idiom from the interview.
speaking.starter: Sam took a risk and… At first, it was… Sam's family raised concerns because… In the end,…

transcript.html: You're listening to The Signal. I'm Nora, and my guest tonight did something most of us only talk about. At forty, Sam walked out of a safe job in accounting and opened a bakery. Sam, welcome.
Thanks, Nora. It's great to be here.
Eighteen years with the same firm. What made you take the risk?

Honestly? I was bitterly disappointed with where I'd ended up. I was good at my job, I always met my deadlines, but I'd stopped making an effort. So I did some research, I ran the numbers, as accountants do, and I drew a conclusion: it was now or never.
And did you hit the ground running?

Not at all. It was a steep learning curve. I knew how to read a balance sheet, but I had no idea how to bake three hundred loaves before six in the morning. In the first month, I cut corners with a cheaper flour, and my customers noticed right away. So it was back to square one.
Let's talk about the elephant in the room. Money. You went from a good salary to, well, what exactly?
To nothing, for the first year. My family raised concerns, and they were right to. It was highly unlikely that I'd ever earn the same again. And I still don't.
That's very candid. So, any regrets?

You know, losing that salary was a blessing in disguise. It forced me to keep the business small and simple. I work harder than I ever did, and on Sunday nights I look forward to Monday. I couldn't say that once in eighteen years.
Sam, thank you. After the break, your calls.

blocks.title: PICK THE PARTNER
blocks.intro: All three options are real English words. Only one is the partner a native speaker expects.

items.q: Sorry, I ___ a mistake in the script.
We need to ___ more research before the show.
It's ___ unlikely that the guest will cancel.
She was ___ disappointed when the show was canceled.
There was ___ traffic, so the guest arrived late.
Several listeners ___ concerns about the new schedule.
There's only a ___ chance that it will rain.

blocks.title: WHAT SOUNDS NATIVE?
blocks.intro: Both sentences are understood. Only one is what a native speaker would say.

items.q: Why is the other one wrong?

options: We drove through a big rain.
Let's do a look at the script.
Let's have a look at the script.
Let's make a look at the script.

blocks.title: SMALL TALK BEFORE THE SHOW
blocks.intro: Sam arrives at the studio and you keep the guest company. Pick the reply with the right word partners.

lines.html: Hi! Sorry I'm a bit late. The traffic was terrible.

options: No problem. Strong traffic is very normal here.
No problem at all. Heavy traffic is perfectly normal at this hour.
Don't worry. The traffic was very big today.

lines.html: Is this your first week here?

options: My first day. It's a steep learning curve, but I'm enjoying it.
My first day. I knew a lot of new people this morning.
My first day. I have a strong learning curve.

lines.html: I'm a little nervous, to be honest. I've never been on the radio.

options: That has sense. Nora will do you feel at home.
It's logic. Nora makes very good questions.
That makes sense. Nora will make you feel at home.

lines.html: Do you know what she's going to ask me?

options: Roughly. She did some research on your story, but she likes to play it by ear.
Roughly. She made a research, but she likes to play by ears.
Roughly. She did researches about you and plays it for ear.
Be yourself. And if you do a mistake, keep going.
Be yourself. And if you make a mistake, keep going.
Be yourself. And if you have a mistake, continue.

blocks.title: AUDIO 2 · THE NOTES
blocks.desc: You drafted an introduction for Sam. Roz sends you a voice memo with her notes: four word partners to fix before Nora reads it on air.

questions.q: How does Roz correct "made a research"?
Which adjective does she want with "traffic"?
What does Roz say about the idioms in the draft?
options: They are used with the wrong meaning
There are too many: keep one

questions.q: What does Roz think of the draft overall?
options: It has to be rewritten from the start
It is ready to go on air
It is close: the idea works, the partners need fixing

speaking.prompt: Record a 30-second introduction for Sam, as Nora would read it. Use three collocations from this lesson.
speaking.starter: My guest tonight took a risk that… After eighteen years, Sam drew a conclusion:… It was highly unlikely that…

transcript.html: Hi, it's Roz. I've read your draft intro for Sam, and it's nearly there. But four word partners need fixing before Nora reads it on air. One. You wrote "Sam made a research." We don't make research. We do research. Two. "He did a big effort." It's "made a big effort." Three. "He got stuck in strong traffic on the way here." Traffic is heavy, not strong. And four. "Sam won a lot of money as an accountant." You win a prize. You earn money. Oh, and one more thing. You've got three idioms in two sentences. Pick one and cut the rest. The idea is good, though, and the story makes sense. Fix those and send it back before five. Thanks!

blocks.title: <ico-pen></ico-pen> THE GUEST INTRO
blocks.intro: Write the introduction Nora will read on air for a guest of your choice: someone you admire, real or invented (about 80 words).
checklist: Three collocations from this lesson (take a risk, raise concerns, highly unlikely…)
The words of the day: candid, hit the ground running or take a risk can count toward the points above
No clichés (think outside the box, at the end of the day)
Check the Spanish traps: ask a question, make a mistake, earn money
blocks.example: My guest tonight who + what they did. At age / moment, name took a risk: the risk. It was highly unlikely that what could go wrong. one sentence with your idiom. Tonight, in a candid conversation, what we will hear. Please welcome name.
blocks.hw: Write your intro, then record yourself reading it like a radio host: slow, warm, with pauses. Send me the text and the audio on WhatsApp.

rubric.d: About 80 words, and it works as an introduction: we know who the guest is and why we should listen.
Three correct collocations, exactly one idiom used with the right meaning, and the words of the day.
A listener understands it without hearing it twice. No word-for-word translation from Spanish.
